contributions.headingText: Prepubertal-type testicular neuroendocrine tumour (NET) is usually a well-differentiated NET of the testis, resembling NETs arising in the gastrointestinal tract.
2F77 & XH8DS0 Neoplasms of uncertain behaviour of male genital organs & Neuroendocrine tumour, NOS
Not recommended: neuroendocrine carcinoma; carcinoid; atypical carcinoid.

A testicular mass or swelling is the most common presenting symptom. A minority of patients may have carcinoid syndrome, with hot flashes, diarrhoea, and palpitations {20351489}. The tumours mostly occur in adults (age range: 10–83 years) and are more common than other germ cell tumours in older patients (mean age: 46 years). Few cases have been reported in children {20351489; 18190641}.

NETs account for < 1% of all testicular tumours {20351489}. They are about 15 times as common in the ovary as in the testicle {18316560}. The majority of NETs have been reported in Europe and the USA, with fewer reported in Asia {26137005; 14516318} and in Africa {30799770}.

These tumours are considered monodermal teratomas. Their histogenesis is a matter of debate, but most are not associated with isochromosome 12p or germ cell neoplasia in situ. Small NETs are seen in association with prepubertal-type teratomas {31695156}. However, occasional cases probably arise in postpubertal-type teratomas {18316560}. Although these may arise from a yet unidentified neuroendocrine cell, the most plausible explanation is that they develop from germ cell–derived intestinal-like neuroendocrine cells {12931547}.

The tumours are solid, circumscribed, and yellow to tan, and they measure 50–110 mm. Sometimes there are calcifications or cystic changes in associated teratomatous areas. Extratesticular growth is uncommon.

Primary testicular NETs can be pure (~75% of cases) or associated with a testicular teratoma (~25%). Most tumours exhibit an insular or trabecular architecture. Acinar and glandular structures with luminal mucin are present, admixed with other patterns. The stroma is usually fibrous to hyalinized. The monomorphic cells contain eosinophilic to pale cytoplasm and uniform round nuclei with fine chromatin. Mitotic figures are rare; necrosis and vascular invasion are infrequently seen. In all but two reported cases, germ cell neoplasia in situ has been absent {16311359; 18316560}.

Immunohistochemistry

The tumour cells express chromogranin A, synaptophysin, serotonin, NSE, CD56, and cytokeratins; less frequently, they express gastrin, substance P, VIP, and neurofilaments. Thyroid transcription factor 1 (TTF1), KIT, CDX2, and OCT3/4 are negative {18316560}. Most are well differentiated, but some that metastasize have atypical features including necrosis and increased mitoses {20351489}. DNA ploidy studies have revealed a near-diploid profile {7688660}. Bilateral involvement, multifocality, and extratesticular localization favour metastasis from the gastrointestinal primary {15667892}. The insular and trabecular patterns of granulosa cell tumour may be confused with NET, but the presence of nuclear grooves and the absence of neuroendocrine markers are useful. Potential pitfalls are Sertoli cell tumours because of their similar growth patterns and often similar immunoreactivity for neuroendocrine markers {20351489}. The characteristic eosinophilic cytoplasm and the salt-and-pepper nuclear pattern are distinctive features of prepubertal-type testicular NETs. α-inhibin, SF1, and β-catenin are positive in Sertoli cell tumours {20351489; 23165333}.

Essential: insular or trabecular architecture; salt-and-pepper pattern of nuclear chromatin.

Desirable: positivity for neuroendocrine markers.

Most primary NETs have a benign clinical course. Atypical NETs are larger tumours with increased mitoses and may be associated with metastases {12931547}. The prognosis of primary testicular NETs associated with a testicular teratoma seems to be better than that of pure NEs {28559773}. The cases associated with carcinoid syndrome have increased metastatic potential {7688660; 20351489}. Patients with malignant tumours show a prolonged clinical course before death. If metastases occur, the haematogenous spread affects the lungs, liver, bones, soft tissue, skin, and heart {18190641}. In patients with metastatic disease, retroperitoneal dissection and receptor-targeted radiotherapy using different isotopes may be used {11870669}. Chemotherapy and radiotherapy provide minimal benefits {15828968}.
